To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the index of microvascular resistance (IMR), a novel index for the evaluation of microcirculation, and coronary flow reserve are both useful to evaluate myocardium viability and long-term prognosis in patients with ST-segment elevation MI (STEMI).

a comprehensive evaluation of microcirculation using the index of microcirulatory resistance and coronary reserve after primary percutanous intervention in ST-segmet elevation myocardial infraction is useful to assess myocardial viability and long-term prognosis of ST-segment elevation mycardial infarction patients.

the comprehensive evaluation of myocardial perfusion by the IMR (a measure of microvascular resistance) and the CFR (a measure of hyperemic flow reserve) immediately after primary PCI is useful in predicting the long-term prognosis after STEMI.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the assessment of microcirculatory function in patients with STEMI.
the assessment of microcirculatory dysfunction in ST-segments myocardial infarctions (STEMI).
the development of a new approach to the study of the microcirculation in the presence of a single-layered layer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the IMR and the CFR are useful tools to evaluate myocardial microcirculation in the acute phase of STEMI, and the microcirculation assessed using both parameters can predict myocardial viability and clinical outcomes.
the combination of CFR and IMR may help to evaluate the microcirculatory status of STEMI patients and predict the long-term prognosis.
microcirculation assessed by the CFR and the IMR is a useful predictor of myocardial viability and a long-term prognosis of patients with STEMI.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a microcirculation of the infarct-related artery in STEMI can be classified into four groups, and that a microcirculatory impairment is associated with a poor prognosis in STEMI.
a microvascular function assessed by the IMR is more important to determine the prognosis of STEMI than the CFR.
the combination of CFR and IMR is useful for the assessment of myocardial viability and long-term prognosis in STEMI patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the IMR and the CFR can complementarily evaluate the microcirculation of the myocardium in STEMI.
microcirculatory assessment using IMR and CFR is useful for evaluating myocardial viability and long-term prognosis of ST-segment elevation acute myocardial infarctions (STEMI).

complimentary assessment of microcirculatory dysfunction by thermodilution IMR and CFR after primary percutaneus coronary intervention in STEMI may be helpful to predict myocardial viability and clinical outcomes.
